column2: As the rising sun shines having removed dense darkness, so a man sprinkled with Ganga water shines having removed sin.
As nights without the moon and trees without flowers, so are countries and directions without the lovely waters of the Ganga.
As the classes and stages without knowledge of their own dharma, and seasons without the moon, so is the world without the Ganga.
As the sky without the sun, the earth without mountains and space without wind, so are countries and directions without the Ganga, without doubt.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, all of them, satisfied with the lovely waters of the Ganga, go to supreme contentment.
One who drinks Ganga water heated by the sun gains what is better than barley freed from cow dung.
One who performs a thousand Indra vows to purify the body and one who drinks Ganga water: they may or may not be equal.
A man who stands a thousand ages on one foot and one who spends one month at the Ganga: they may or may not be equal.
One who hangs head downward for ten thousand ages and one who stays at the Ganga as he wishes: the latter is distinguished.
As cotton thrown into fire is burnt off, best of the twice-born, so all sin of one who plunges into the Ganga is burnt off.
For all beings here whose minds are struck by sorrow and who seek a goal, there is no goal like the Ganga.
As serpents become poisonless at the sight of Garuda, so by the sight of the Ganga one is freed from all sins.
For those who have no support and those who have unrighteousness as refuge, the Ganga here is the support, refuge, happiness and armour.
The lowest of men seized by many evils and falling into hell, if they have taken refuge in the Ganga, she would carry across after death.
Those who always go to the Ganga that has come with the gods are surely shared out by sages and by gods with Vasava.
Even the lowest of men, devoid of discipline and conduct and inauspicious, become auspicious, Brahmana, if they take refuge in the Ganga.
As nectar is for the gods and svadha for the ancestors, and as ambrosia is for the nagas, so Ganga water is for men.
As children afflicted by hunger wait on their mother, so embodied beings who wish for good wait on the Ganga here.
As the Self-born in his place is said to be best of all, so the Ganga is said here to be the best of rivers for the bathed.
As the cow is for those who live by her, and earth is remembered for gods and others, so the Ganga is for all who bear life here.
As the gods live on the nectar placed in the moon and sun by sacrifices and sessions, so men live on Ganga water.
A man smeared with the sand risen on the banks of the Jahnavi thinks himself shining as if in heaven.
He who bears on his head the earth born on the bank of the Jahnavi bears the spotless form of the sun by the destruction of darkness.
When the wind, anointed with waves of the Ganga, touches a man, he too at once wipes away sin.
For a man tormented by misfortunes and about to perish, the joy born of seeing the Ganga draws out the misfortunes.
With the cries of swans, the cries of chakravakas and the cries of other birds, the Ganga rivalled the gandharvas, and with her banks the heaps of rock.
Seeing the Ganga surrounded by swans and many other kinds of birds, crowded with herds of cows, even heaven is forgotten.
The highest joy that men have on the bank of the Ganga is not that joy of one in heaven enjoying all desires.
Even a man seized here by sins born of speech, mind and deed would be purified by seeing the Ganga; of that I have no doubt.
A man carries across seven ancestors before and seven after, and those beyond them, by seeing, touching and plunging into the Ganga.
Heard, desired, seen, touched, drunk and bathed in, the Ganga carries men across, especially both lineages.
By sight, touch, drinking, and by saying "Ganga," she purifies sinful men by hundreds and thousands.
One who wishes his birth, life and learning to be fruitful should go to the Ganga and satisfy ancestors and gods.
A man would not by sons, by wealth, or by deeds gain that fruit utterly which he would gain on reaching the Ganga.
Those who, though able, do not see the Ganga of holy water and good fortune are like the blind from birth here, like the dead and the lame.
What man would not serve the Ganga, attended by great sages who know past, present and future and by gods with Indra?
What man indeed would not take refuge in the Ganga, resorted to by forest-dwellers, householders, ascetics, students and the learned?
One who, as his breaths depart, restrained and approved by the good, thinks of the Ganga in mind would gain the highest goal.
He has no fear from fears, nor from sins, nor from the king, the man who here serves the Ganga until the fall of his body.
The greatly holy goddess whom Maheshvara bore on his head as she fell from the sky: her he serves in heaven.
The three worlds are adorned with her three pure paths; a man who serves her water would become one whose task is done.
As the sun is the light in heaven, the moon for the ancestors and the lord of the gods for men, so is the Ganga among rivers here.
For one separated from mother, father, sons, wife or wealth, there is not such sorrow as that born of separation from the Ganga.
Neither forests, nor desired objects, nor sons, nor gains of wealth bring such serenity to men as seeing the Ganga.
As men's eyes brighten on seeing the full moon, so the eye brightens on seeing the Ganga going by three paths.
One who follows the Ganga with devotion, his being, mind, end and refuge in her, would go to her dearness.
By beings on earth, in the sky and in heaven, high and low, the Ganga is always to be plunged into; this is the most important duty of the good.
The Ganga's fame in the three worlds is made known by her holiness, that she brought the ashes of Sagara's sons to heaven.
Kindled by the Ganga's waves, driven by the wind, of great noise, swift, exceedingly high and lit by the sun, she shines like the thousand-rayed.
Those who, having gone to the Ganga, rich in water and ghee, most generous, prosperous, swift and hard to plunge into, gave up their bodies, those steady ones went to equality with the gods.
The Ganga, glorious, great, of universal form, joins the blind, the dull and the penniless; served by the gods with Indra, by sages and men, she grants all desires.
Those who took refuge in the Ganga, vigorous, honey-sweet, greatly holy, going by three paths and protector of the three worlds, have gone to heaven.
To the mortal who will live by her or see her the gods give joys; to him who is formed by her in touch and sight the gods grant the desired goal.
Those who have gone to the Ganga, skilful, earthly, great, far-spreading, auspicious, true, sweet-juiced, very serene, night-lit, the foundation of all beings, have gone to the third heaven.
Whose fame, always across sky, heaven and earth, stood before in the directions and sub-directions: serving the water of that best of rivers, all mortals become those whose task is done.
This is the Ganga, the fixed foundation; the wife of Guha, the womb of gold; threefold-pathed in the morning, bearer of ghee, sinless, the Ganga came down from the sky with water on every side.
Wife of Shiva, daughter of the mountain, suited to the sphere of heaven and earth, she shines, lovely, king, the destined one of the earth; the Ganga gives merit to the three worlds.
With honey streams, adorned with great waves red like ghee, and by brahmanas, fallen from the sky, taken on the head: the Ganga mountains are the garland of the third heaven.
Best womb, spotless, expanding, strong, Ira, water-bearer, giver of fame, universal, form, wish, bright, the path to the world for those sprinkled by the Ganga.
In forgiveness she equals the earth; in protecting and bearing, in brightness fire and sun; the Ganga is approved by brahmanas, and always by Guha's regard for brahmanas.
Those who with their whole selves go to the Jahnavi, praised by sages, the footstep of Vishnu, ancient, of most holy water, even in thought in the world, have gone to Brahma's abode.

She who leads these worlds like a mother her sons, endowed with all qualities with her whole self, the Ganga is always to be served by those who have mastered themselves and wish their own Brahmanic place here.

The self-possessed who desires success should resort to the Ganga, ray-like, served, shining, with water everywhere, Ira, thunderbolt-bearing, Revati of the mountains, refuge of the good, immortal, beloved of Brahman.
Having pleased all the lords of gods, Bhagiratha by fierce austerity brought the Ganga to earth; going to her always, a man would know no fear here or hereafter.
One part of her qualities has been told by me, having considered with understanding; I have no power here to tell all the qualities or to measure them.
One could tell the jewels of Meru and the sea, the number of stones or the water, but one cannot here tell or measure the qualities of the Ganga's waters.
Therefore these qualities told with supreme faith, and all those born of the Jahnavi, one should reach in speech, mind and deed, joined with devotion, believing.
Having spread over these three worlds by fame and gained that great hard success, you will soon roam as you wish the desired worlds made by the Ganga.
The gleaner, enlightened then by the perfected one's words, served the Ganga by rule and gained the very hard success.
Therefore you too, Kaunteya, joined with supreme devotion, go constantly to the Ganga; you will gain the highest success.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing the Itihasa told by Bhishma with the praise of the Ganga, Yudhishthira with his brothers gained supreme joy.
One who hears or reads this holy Itihasa joined with the praise of the Ganga would be freed from all sins.
[Yudhishthira said:] A kshatriya, a vaishya, or a shudra, best of kings, by what could he gain brahminhood? You ought to tell me.
By great austerity, or deed, or learning: if one should wish brahminhood, tell me that, grandfather.
[Bhishma said:] Brahminhood, dear one, is hard to get for the three classes beginning with kshatriya; it is the highest place of all beings, Yudhishthira.
Passing through many wombs, being born again and again, in some turn, dear one, one is born a brahmana.
On this they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Matanga and a she-donkey, Yudhishthira.
A certain twice-born had a son, of equal class, powerful, named Matanga, endowed with all qualities.
He, a sacrificial performer, Kaunteya, sent by his father, went on a swift chariot yoked with donkeys.
He struck again and again on the nose with a goad a young donkey, O king, that was pulling near its mother.
Seeing that severely wounded one, the she-donkey, fond of her son, said: "Do not grieve, son; a Chandala is driving you.
There is no cruelty in a brahmana; a brahmana is called friendly, teacher of all beings, protector; what will he strike?
But this one is of sinful nature and has no mercy on a child; he honours his own womb; feeling goes to feeling."
Hearing the donkey's harsh words, Matanga quickly got down from the chariot and said to the she-donkey:

Tell me, fair she-donkey, how you know me as a Chandala by whom my mother is defiled; say it quickly.
mahabharata:13:28.15	By whom am I born a Chandala, by whom was my brahminhood lost? Tell me all this in truth, greatly wise one, without remainder.
[The she-donkey said:] "You were born of a brahmin woman intoxicated, by a shudra barber; you are a Chandala, and therefore your brahminhood was lost."
Thus addressed, Matanga returned home; seeing him come, his father spoke these words:
I appointed you for the accomplishment of the sacrifice in the teacher's work; why have you turned back? I hope you are well.
[Matanga said:] "One who is of no womb or of a fine womb is well; how can he be well whose mother is this, father?
Father, this she-donkey, not human, tells me here that I was born of a brahmin woman by a shudra; therefore I shall practise great austerity."
Having so spoken to his father, he set out resolved, then went to a great forest and practised great austerity.
Then, joined with austerity, he distressed the gods, Matanga, wishing a happy place from good conduct.
To him, thus joined with austerity, the lord whose steeds are bay horses said: "Matanga, why do you practise austerity, giving up human enjoyments?
I shall give you a boon; choose whatever you wish, and whatever else is to be obtained by you, tell it all quickly."
[Matanga said:] "Wishing brahminhood I began this austerity; may I go and gain it here. This boon is chosen by me."
Hearing this, Purandara said to him: "You, seeking brahminhood, ask what is unattainable to the unpractised.
You seek that best state among all beings, austerity that does not pass beyond; you will soon perish.
What is remembered as the supreme holiness among gods, asuras and mortals cannot in any way be got by one born in a Chandala womb."
Then the greatly famous Shakra spoke again to him, Matanga, who asked for a supreme, very hard state:

Do not be rash, son; this is not the path of dharma; seeking the unattainable you will soon perish.
mahabharata:13:29.4	Matanga, though I forbid you once from the supreme state, you wish to do it by austerity, but in every way you will not become so.
mahabharata:13:29.5	One who has gone to an animal womb, if he goes to the human state, is sometimes born a Pulkasa or a Chandala.
mahabharata:13:29.6	Whoever is seen here as a whore or of a sinful womb, Matanga, turns about in that very state for a long time.
mahabharata:13:29.7	Then in ten times that time he gains the state of a shudra, and again turns about many times in the shudra womb.
mahabharata:13:29.8	Then in thirty times that time he gains the state of a vaishya, and turns about in the vaishya state for a long time.
mahabharata:13:29.9	Then in sixty times that time he is born a kshatriya, and turns about in the kshatriya state for a long time.
mahabharata:13:29.12	Then in three hundred times that time he gains twice-bornness, and having reached it turns about there a long time.
mahabharata:13:29.13	Then in four hundred times that time he is born a Shrotriya, and turns about in that state a long time.
mahabharata:13:29.14	Then, son, anger and joy, desire and hatred, excessive pride and slander enter that lowest of the twice-born.
mahabharata:13:29.15	If he conquers those enemies, then he gains a good goal; but if they conquer him, he falls as if from the top of a palm.
mahabharata:13:29.16	Matanga, consider this which I have told you; choose another wish, for brahminhood is very hard.
[Bhishma said:] Bearing very hard yoga, lean, with veins showing, skin and bone, the righteous-souled one fell: so we have heard.
Rushing at him as he fell, Vasava took hold of him, lord of boons, giver, delighting in the good of all beings.
[Shakra said:] "Matanga, your brahminhood is hindered by enemies; honouring brings happiness, not honouring brings sorrow.
In a brahmana the welfare and security of all beings is composed; from brahmanas ancestors and gods are satisfied.
A brahmana is called the highest of all beings, Matanga; a brahmana does that as and what he wishes.
Passing through many wombs, being born again and again, in some turn, dear one, one finds brahminhood here."
[Matanga said:] "Why do you torment me, afflicted by sorrow, and kill me who am dead? I grieve for him who, having got brahminhood, does not wish to be so.
If brahminhood is hard to gain for the three classes, Shatakratu, very rare, men who have got it do not practise it."

Alone in my pleasure, Shakra, free of pairs, without possessions, standing in non-violence, self-control and giving, why am I not fit for brahminhood?
mahabharata:13:30.13	Let me be a wanderer at will, a bird that takes any form, and let me gain honour without conflict between brahmin and kshatriya, and let my fame be imperishable, Purandara.
[Indra said:] "You will be famed as Chhandodeva and be honoured by women."
[Bhishma said:] Having so given him a boon, Vasava vanished, and Matanga, giving up his breath, gained that highest place.
Thus this supreme state called brahminhood is, Bharata, hard to get, as Mahendra's word says.
[Yudhishthira said:] It is heard that Vishvamitra also long ago gained brahminhood; and you say it is hard to get, good one.
I have heard that the royal sage Vitahavya attained brahminhood; I wish to hear that, Gangeya, lord.
By what deed did that best of kings gain brahminhood, by a boon or by austerity? You ought to tell me.
[Bhishma said:] Hear, king, how King Vitahavya of great fame, though a kshatriya, again gained brahminhood honoured by the world.
When the great-souled Manu ruled his subjects with dharma, a son was born, righteous-souled, famed as Sharyati.
In his line two kings were born, king: Haihaya and Talajangha, in the Vatsa country, best of the victorious.
Of Haihaya's sons by ten wives, Bharata, a hundred were famed, heroes who did not turn back,
of equal form and power, learned, skilled in battle, trained everywhere in the science of the bow and in the Veda.
Knowing the might of those great souls, Divodasa of great splendour, by Shakra's command, built Varanasi.
Crowded with brahmanas and kshatriyas, full of vaishyas and shudras, with heaps of many goods, with prosperous markets and shops,
on the north bank of the Ganga, at the edge of the rampart, best of kings, and south of the Gomati, like Shakra's Amaravati.
The Haihayas came again there to the best of kings living there, Bharata, and ran around him.
Going out, the mighty king Divodasa, of great splendour, fought them in a terrible battle like that of gods and asuras.
In that battle, great king, for ten times ten days, with most of his vehicles slain, he then came to dejection.
His warriors slain and his treasury spent, the king Divodasa, leaving the city, turned to flight.
Coming to the hermitage of the wise Bharadvaja, the king, scourge of foes, with joined palms took refuge.
[The king said:] "Blessed one, my line has been destroyed in battle by the Vitahavyas; I alone am left, distressed, come to you for refuge.
Out of affection for a pupil, blessed one, you ought to protect me; my line has been made without remainder by those sinful ones."
The greatly fortunate and mighty Bharadvaja said to him: "Do not fear, do not fear, Sudeva; let your fear depart.
Today I perform a sacrifice for a son for you, lord of men, so that you may overcome thousands of Vitahavyas."
Then the sage performed the sacrifice for a son for him; and a son was born to him, famed as Pratardana.
As soon as born, he grew thirteen years at once, and learned the entire Veda and the science of the bow, Bharata.
Joined by the wise Bharadvaja with yoga, he gathered the splendour of the world and entered that country.
Then, armoured, with bow and arrows, blazing like fire, he set out with his bow like a rain-cloud about to rain.
Seeing him, Sudeva's son came to supreme joy, and the king thought the Vitahavyas burnt in his mind.
Then, having established Pratardana as heir apparent, that king rejoiced, thinking himself one whose task was done.
Then the king sent his son Pratardana, scourge of foes, for the slaying of the Vitahavyas.
On his chariot, the mighty conqueror of enemy cities quickly crossed the Ganga and set out to the city of the Vitahavyas.
Hearing the roar of his chariot rising, the Vitahavyas came out in chariots like cities, breakers of enemy chariots.
Coming out, those tigers among men, armoured, fighting in varied ways, with weapons raised, struck Pratardana with showers of arrows.
With weapons of many kinds and masses of chariots, Yudhishthira, they rained on the king like clouds on the Himalaya.
Countering their weapons with weapons, King Pratardana of great splendour slew them with arrows like thunderbolt and fire.
Their heads cut off by lances, king, hundreds of thousands fell, their limbs wet with blood, cut down like kimshuka trees.
When all his sons were slain, Vitahavya fled, leaving the city, and went to Bhrigu's hermitage.
King Vitahavya went to Bhrigu for refuge, and Bhrigu gave that king safety; and then Bhrigu's pupil gave him a seat.
Then right behind him Pratardana quickly came there; reaching the hermitage, Divodasa's son said:
Ho, ho! Who are in this hermitage, pupils of the great-souled Bhrigu? I wish to see the sage; tell him of me.
Knowing him, Bhrigu then came out of the hermitage and honoured him by rule highly.
He said to the king, "What is your business?" and the king told him the reason for his coming.

Brahmana, let this king Vitahavya be released from here. By his sons my whole line was destroyed, and the country of the Kashis, a store of jewels, was uprooted.
mahabharata:13:31.48	His hundred sons, proud of valour, have been slain by me; by killing him now, Brahmana, I shall be free of debt to my father.
Moved by pity, Bhrigu, best of upholders of dharma, said to him: "There is no kshatriya here; all these are twice-born."
Hearing Bhrigu's true word, Pratardana touched his feet and, laughing gently, said:

Even so, blessed one, I am one whose task is done, without doubt, since by my valour this king was made to give up his class.
mahabharata:13:31.52	Give me leave, Brahmana, and meditate on me with good will; for I have made this king lose his class, lifter of Bhrigu's line.
Permitted by him, King Pratardana went as he came, great king, like a serpent leaving poison.
By Bhrigu's word alone, Vitahavya became a Brahmarishi, great king, and a speaker of Brahman.
His son Gritsamada, like another Indra in form, was once seized by the Daityas, thinking "You are Shakra."
In the Rig Veda is a foremost hymn, lord of men, where Gritsamada is honoured by brahmanas, Brahmana.
That glorious brahmana sage Gritsamada was a celibate student, and Gritsamada's son was the twice-born Sucheta.
Varcha was the son of Sutejas, Vihavya his son; and Vitatya was Vihavya's son, and Vitatya's son.
Vitatya's son was Satya, Santa Satya's son; his son the sage Shrava, and Shravasa's Tamas.
Prakasha was born as Tamas's son, best of the twice-born, and Prakasha's son was Vagindra, best of the victorious.
His son was Pramati, who had crossed the Vedas and Vedangas; by Ghritachi his son named Ruru was born.
By Pramadvara a son was born to Ruru, the brahmana sage named Shunaka, whose son was Shaunaka.
Thus King Vitahavya attained brahminhood by Bhrigu's grace, king of kings, a kshatriya, bull among kshatriyas.
So the lineage of Gritsamada's family has been told to you in detail, great king; what else do you ask?
[Bhishma said:] On this too they recite this ancient Itihasa, the conversation of Narada and Vasudeva, both.
Seeing Narada with joined palms worshipping the bulls among the twice-born, Keshava asked: "Blessed one, whom do you salute?
In whom is your highest regard, whom you salute? If it can be heard, I wish to hear this, best of knowers of dharma."
[Narada said:] "Hear, Govinda, those whom I worship, scourge of foes; what man in the world other than you is fit to hear this here?
Varuna, Vayu, Aditya, Parjanya, Agni, Sthanu, Skanda, Lakshmi, Vishnu and Brahma,
Vachaspati, the moon, the waters, the earth and Sarasvati: those who always salute these I salute, lord.
Ascetics, knowers of the Veda, always devoted to the Veda, the greatly worthy, tiger of the Vrishnis, I always worship.
Those who, not boasting, perform the acts of the gods without eating first, contented and joined with forgiveness: those I salute, lord.
Those of calm heart toward all beings always, joined to study until the back is heated: those I worship.
Those of firm vows who strive in the teacher's grace and in study, desiring to serve and without envy: those I salute, Yadava.
Sages of good vows, friends of brahmanas, true to their pledges, bearers of offerings to gods and ancestors: those I salute, Yadava.
Those devoted to the practice of begging alms, lean, dwelling in teachers' houses, joyless and wealthless: those I salute, Yadava.
Those without mine-ness, without rivals, without shame, without purpose, devoted to non-violence, men of true vows, self-controlled and intent on peace: those I salute, Keshava.
Householders devoted to the worship of gods and guests, living always like doves: those I salute, Yadava.
Those whose three aims are pursued in their duties and not lost, and who follow the conduct of the good: those I always salute.
Brahmanas in the three worlds who follow the three aims, ungreedy and of meritorious conduct: those I salute, Keshava.
Those who always live on water, on air, or on nectar, and are joined with various vows: those I salute, Madhava.
Those twice-born whose wombs are none, whose wombs are fire, whose wombs are Brahman, and whose wombs are the self of all beings: those I salute."
I went to the son of Angiras, Brihaspati, teacher of the gods, to see him as officiant for the sacrifice, and he did not welcome me.
Then the king of great splendour said to the son of Dharma: "Permitted by you, son, I wish to eat."
Going to the abode of the Vrishnis with Daruka, the hero saw Dvaraka like a woman whose lord is dead.
Then in another place he saw the lord Bhimasena, surrounded by hosts of Maruts, with the same body as before.
